title: Level 2 – Cyber Explorer (Year 8)
_about: Written by Anish Shrestha (2) and Kiri Rāwiri (simulated). Draft for Cultural Guide review. Categories: PHISH, SPOOF, PRIV, PWD.

questions.text: What is phishing?

options.B: A message that pretends to be from someone trusted to steal information
options.D: A way to speed up Wi-Fi

questions.feedback: Phishing messages pretend to be real so you click, log in or pay. Always check before you act.

questions.text: Which of these are warning signs of a phishing message? Choose ALL that apply.

options.A: It says your account will be closed today
options.B: It offers a free prize you never entered
options.C: It asks you to confirm your password with a link
options.D: It is from your teacher on the school app about tomorrow's homework

questions.feedback: Urgency, prizes and requests for passwords are classic warning signs. A normal homework note in the school app is not.

questions.scenario_text: A text says: "You have an unpaid toll road fee of $4.80. Pay within 24 hours to avoid a fine: nz-toll-payment.top". Your family drove on a toll road last month.
questions.text: What is the safest action?

options.A: Pay through the link because you did use a toll road
options.B: Forward it to friends to warn them by clicking first
options.D: Ask an adult to check by going to the official website or app themselves

questions.feedback: Scammers send fake toll messages to many people. Check by typing the official address yourself – never pay through the link.

questions.text: A game message offers 10,000 free coins if you log in on a website it links to. What is most likely happening?

options.A: Someone is trying to steal your game login

questions.feedback: Free currency offers are a common trick to steal gaming accounts. Only log in through the real game or app.

questions.text: True or false: scams can be reported to the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) in New Zealand.
questions.feedback: The NCSC (which now includes CERT NZ) collects reports of scams and cyber incidents and gives advice.

questions.scenario_text: A social media post says the local marae is raising money for a new roof. It asks people to send their bank card number by private message. The marae has never posted from this account before.
questions.text: What should you and your whānau do?

options.A: Send the card number to help quickly
options.B: Share the post so more people donate
options.C: Check with the marae committee using a contact you already know

questions.feedback: Scammers copy real community causes. Never send card numbers by message – check with the marae directly.

questions.scenario_text: An email shows the sender name "Inland Revenue" but the address is refunds@ird-nz-refund.com. It asks you to click a link to get money back.
questions.text: What shows it is fake?

options.B: The sender's domain is not the official ird.govt.nz

questions.feedback: Check the real domain. Official New Zealand government websites end in govt.nz.

questions.text: What is email spoofing?

options.A: Sending an email with a fake sender so it looks like it came from someone else

questions.feedback: Spoofed emails fake the sender. Always look at the real address, not just the display name.

questions.text: True or false: if a website has a padlock (HTTPS), it must be a safe and honest website.
questions.feedback: The padlock only means the connection is encrypted. Scam websites can have padlocks too.

questions.text: Which web address is most likely a fake copy of a real site?
questions.feedback: "micros0ft" uses a zero instead of the letter o and adds "-login". Small changes like this are a common trick.

questions.text: What is the safest way to visit your bank or school portal?

options.B: Search and click the first ad
options.C: Type the address yourself or use a saved bookmark
options.D: Use a link a stranger sent

questions.feedback: Typing the address or using a bookmark avoids fake links.

questions.text: What is a digital footprint?

options.B: The trail of information you leave online

questions.feedback: Posts, photos, comments and searches all add to your digital footprint.

questions.scenario_text: Mere wants to post a photo outside her house. The photo shows her school uniform, her street sign and a location tag.
questions.text: What is the best advice for Mere?

options.B: Post it publicly so more people see it
options.C: Remove the location tag and choose a photo that does not show her street or school

questions.feedback: Uniforms, street signs and location tags can show strangers where you live and go to school.

questions.scenario_text: Your cousin wants to post photos from a family funeral (tangihanga) on a public social media page.
questions.text: What is the most respectful thing to do?

options.A: Ask the whānau first, because some images are tapu (sacred) and private
options.B: Post them – they are nice photos
options.C: Post them and remove later if someone complains

questions.feedback: Some information and images are tapu or very personal for families. Always ask your whānau before sharing.

questions.text: Which actions protect your privacy on social media? Choose ALL that apply.
questions.feedback: Private accounts, no location sharing and regular checks help. Accepting everyone lets strangers in.

questions.text: True or false: deleting a post means nobody can ever see it again.
questions.feedback: Someone may have taken a screenshot or saved it before you deleted it. Think before you post.

questions.text: Which is an example of password mismanagement?

options.D: Writing your password on a sticky note on the screen

questions.feedback: Anyone who walks past can read a sticky note on your screen.

questions.scenario_text: You get a message: "Oops! I sent my login code to your number by mistake. Can you send it back to me?"
questions.text: What should you do?

options.A: Send the code – they asked nicely
options.B: Do not send it; it is a trick to take over your account

questions.feedback: One-time codes are like keys. Real people and companies never need yours.

questions.text: What does a password manager do?

options.A: Stores long, different passwords safely for you
options.C: Makes all your passwords the same

questions.feedback: A password manager remembers strong, unique passwords so you do not have to.

questions.text: A website you use says it was hacked. What should you do first?

options.C: Change that password, and any other account that used the same password

questions.feedback: Change the password straight away – and anywhere else you reused it.

questions.text: True or false: turning on two-step verification (MFA) can stop someone logging in even if they know your password.
questions.feedback: MFA adds a second check that a thief usually does not have.

questions.text: Which are good account recovery options for a Year 8 student? Choose ALL that apply.

options.C: A stranger's email from a game
options.D: Backup codes kept somewhere safe at home

questions.feedback: Recovery options should belong to you or a trusted adult. Never use a stranger's contact.
